title: The Hittite language was cracked in 1915 with one line about bread and water
body: On 8 October 2026 Turkey’s culture minister announced 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments found this year at Kayalıpınar, the Hittite city of Samuha, which make a [royal archive of 184](https://www.dailysabah.com/life/hittite-royal-archive-with-184-tablets-unearthed-in-central-turkiye/news) from the reign of King Tudhaliya II, about 3,400 years old. They can be read because of how cuneiform works: each sign, a cluster of wedges pressed into clay, can stand for a syllable, for a whole word borrowed from Sumerian, or be a silent label, like the sign for “city” before a city’s name. When tablets in an unknown language came out of the Hittite capital, Hattusa, from 1906, scholars could sound them out but not understand them. In 1915 the Czech scholar [Bedřich Hrozný](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bed%C5%99ich_Hrozn%C3%BD) took the line *nu NINDA-an ezzatteni watar-ma ekutteni*: NINDA was the known Sumerian sign for bread, ezza- looked like Latin edo and German essen, and watar like English water. “You will eat bread; you will drink water” showed that Hittite is an Indo-European language, a relative of English, German and Latin, and the oldest of the family on record.

slides.question: Hittite scribes wrote in cuneiform borrowed from Akkadian. How many different signs does a standard list count?
slides.explanation: 375, in the standard sign list of Hittite, the Hethitisches Zeichenlexikon. Old Assyrian used some 600; the English alphabet has 26 letters.

slides.alt: Animation on dark slate: a terracotta clay tablet filling with wedges, 53 plus 131 makes 184, a reed pressing wedges into clay, a grid of 375 signs, sign cards for a syllable, a word sign and a silent label, Hattusa spelled out, Hrozný’s line with its meanings, and the Indo-European family.

slides.prompt: Read Bedřich Hrozný’s line of 1915 as he did: tap each unknown word, then the meaning its look-alikes point to.
slides.takeaway: “You will eat bread; you will drink water.” One known Sumerian sign, NINDA, and three words that looked like Latin, German and English showed that Hittite is Indo-European.

slides.heading: One sign, three jobs
slides.text: The same cluster of wedges can do different work. The sign GI, for instance, is the syllable gi, the Akkadian spelling of a word for “near”, and the Sumerian word sign for “tube”. Silent labels sort nouns into classes: DINGIR goes before gods, URU before cities, LÚ before men. Readers tell the jobs apart from context.

events.text: Hittite is written on clay in cuneiform
Royal archives in an unknown language are found at Hattusa
Bedřich Hrozný shows that Hittite is Indo-European
Kayalıpınar’s archive reaches 184 tablets and fragments

slides.question: Why was the sign NINDA the key to Bedřich Hrozný’s reading of Hittite in 1915?
options: Its meaning, bread, was already known
It was the only syllable sign
It is the Hittite word for water
It was written in Greek letters
slides.explanation: NINDA is a Sumerian word sign for bread, readable without knowing Hittite. Next to it, ezza- looked like Latin edo and German essen: “you (will) eat bread”.
